worked_solution: (a) "A only if B" means A → B, so the statement is q → p
(b) "yet" means and, so it is ¬p ∧ q
(c) Rewrite the implication as an or: q → p ≡ ¬q ∨ p
Rewrite the other one the same way: ¬p → ¬q ≡ ¬(¬p) ∨ ¬q ≡ p ∨ ¬q
p ∨ ¬q and ¬q ∨ p are the same by commutativity, so the two are equivalent (q → p is the contrapositive of ¬p → ¬q)

prompt_parts.text: Build the truth table of (p ∨ q) → ¬r. In how many of the 8 rows is it false?

worked_solution: An implication is false only when the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false
Conclusion ¬r is false exactly when r = T
With r = T, the hypothesis p ∨ q is true for (p,q) = (T,T), (T,F), (F,T) and false for (F,F)
So the false rows (p,q,r) are TTT, TFT, FTT
The other 5 rows are true
final_answer: False in exactly 3 of the 8 rows: TTT, TFT, FTT

Inductive hypothesis: assume Σ_{k=1}^{m} k(k + 1) = m(m + 1)(m + 2)/3 for some m ≥ 1
Add the next term: Σ_{k=1}^{m+1} = m(m + 1)(m + 2)/3 + (m + 1)(m + 2)
= (m + 1)(m + 2)(m + 3)/3, which is the formula with n = m + 1
By induction the formula holds for all n ≥ 1

worked_solution: Base cases (four of them, because the step reaches back 4): 12 = 4·3 + 5·0, 13 = 4·2 + 5·1
Inductive step: let n ≥ 16 and assume every k with 12 ≤ k < n has the form 4a + 5b
n − 4 ≥ 12 and n − 4 < n, so n − 4 = 4a + 5b for some a, b ≥ 0
Then n = 4(a + 1) + 5b with a + 1, b ≥ 0
So every n ≥ 12 works (and 11 does not, so 12 is the best start)
final_answer: Every n ≥ 12 equals 4a + 5b with a, b ≥ 0

prompt_latex: a_1=1,\ a_2=3,\ a_n=a_{n-1}+2a_{n-2}.\ \text{Prove by strong induction that } a_n=\dfrac{2^{n+1}+(-1)^n}{3}.

worked_solution: Inductive step: let n ≥ 3 and assume the formula for n − 1 and n − 2
The powers of 2 add: 2ⁿ + 2·2^(n−1) = 2ⁿ + 2ⁿ = 2^(n+1)
So aₙ = (2^(n+1) + (−1)ⁿ)/3, completing the step

prompt_latex: \text{Prove by induction that } 3^n\ge n^2 \text{ for all } n\ge0. \text{ Why do you need three base cases?}

prompt_parts.text: Prove by induction that 3ⁿ ≥ n² for all n ≥ 0. Why do you need base cases up to n = 2?

worked_solution: Base cases: n = 0: 1 ≥ 0; n = 1: 3 ≥ 1; n = 2: 9 ≥ 4. All true ✓
Inductive hypothesis: assume 3^m ≥ m² for some m ≥ 2
For m ≥ 2, 2m² ≥ 2m + 1 (since 2m² − 2m − 1 = 2m(m − 1) − 1 ≥ 3 for m ≥ 2)
The step needs m ≥ 2: at m = 1 the middle inequality 3m² ≥ (m + 1)² would say 3 ≥ 4, which is false. So n = 2 is checked by hand, and so are n = 0 and n = 1, which lie below where the step starts
final_answer: 3ⁿ ≥ n² for all n ≥ 0; the inductive step only works from m = 2

prompt_latex: T(1)=0,\ T(n)=2T(n/2)+n \text{ for } n=2^k.\ \text{Find a closed form and } T(16).

worked_solution: After j levels: T(n) = 2^j T(n/2^j) + j·n
Stop at j = k where n/2^k = 1, so T(n) = 2^k·T(1) + k·n = k·n
With k = log₂ n: T(n) = n log₂ n
final_answer: T(n) = n log₂ n, so T(16) = 64

prompt_latex: \text{Show that any 6 different numbers chosen from } \{1,\dots,10\} \text{ contain two that add to 11.}

prompt_parts.text: Show that any 6 different numbers chosen from {1, …, 10} contain two that add to 11.

worked_solution: Make pigeonholes from pairs that sum to 11: {1,10}, {2,9}, {3,8}, {4,7}, {5,6}
That is 5 holes and every number from 1 to 10 sits in exactly one
Six different numbers go into 5 holes, so by the pigeonhole principle some hole gets two of them
Those two numbers fill the whole hole, so they are the pair and add to 11
final_answer: Some pair {k, 11 − k} must be chosen, so two chosen numbers sum to 11

worked_solution: Reflexive: (1,1), (2,2), (3,3), (4,4) are all in R ✓
Symmetric: (1,2) ↔ (2,1) and (3,4) ↔ (4,3) both present ✓

Transitive: a chain that uses a pair (a,a) just returns the other pair, so nothing new. The chains of two different pairs are (1,2),(2,1) → (1,1) ✓, (2,1),(1,2) → (2,2) ✓, (3,4),(4,3) → (3,3) ✓, (4,3),(3,4) → (4,4) ✓; all are in R
final_answer: R is an equivalence relation with classes {1, 2} and {3, 4}

prompt_latex: \text{On the positive integers let } a\,R\,b \iff a \mid b. \text{ Decide reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive.}

prompt_parts.text: On the positive integers let a R b mean a divides b. Decide whether R is reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive.

worked_solution: Reflexive: a | a for every a ✓
Symmetric: 2 | 4 but 4 ∤ 2, so no ✗
Antisymmetric: if a | b and b | a with a, b > 0 then a ≤ b and b ≤ a, so a = b ✓
Transitive: if b = ak and c = bm then c = a(km), so a | c ✓
Reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive: R is a partial order
final_answer: Reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive; not symmetric (a partial order)

worked_solution: Row i, column j is 1 if (i,j) ∈ R: row 1 = [0 1 0], row 2 = [0 0 1], row 3 = [1 0 1]
Not reflexive: (1,1) is missing (diagonal has a 0)
Not irreflexive: (3,3) is in R (diagonal has a 1)

Not transitive: (1,2) and (2,3) are in R but (1,3) is not
final_answer: Only antisymmetric; not reflexive, irreflexive, symmetric or transitive

prompt_latex: \text{Design a finite-state machine (DFA) that accepts exactly the binary strings ending in 01. Give the transition table and trace } 110101.
prompt_plain: Design a finite-state machine (DFA) that accepts exactly the binary strings ending in 01. Give the transition table and trace the input 110101.

prompt_parts.text: Design a finite-state machine (DFA) that accepts exactly the binary strings ending in 01. Give the transition table and trace the input 110101.

worked_solution: States: q0 = start, or the last symbol was a 1 that did not follow a 0; q1 = last symbol was 0; q2 = last two symbols were 01 (accepting)
q0: on 0 go to q1, on 1 stay at q0
q1: on 0 stay at q1, on 1 go to q2
q2: on 0 go to q1 (the new 0 may start another 01), on 1 go to q0
Transition table (state: on 0, on 1): q0: q1, q0.  q1: q1, q2.  q2: q1, q0
Ends in q2, the accepting state, so 110101 is accepted (it does end in 01)
final_answer: Table (on 0, on 1): q0: q1, q0; q1: q1, q2; q2: q1, q0; accept q2; 110101 is accepted

Each use of S → aSb adds one a on the left and one b on the right
The final step S → ab ends the string, so we always get equal numbers of a's then b's
Language = { aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1 }
aab has 2 a's and 1 b, so it is not of the form aⁿbⁿ and is not generated
This grammar is context-free (one non-terminal on the left)
final_answer: L(G) = {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}; aaabbb is in it, aab is not

prompt_latex: \text{A simple graph is 3-regular (every vertex has degree 3) with 12 edges. How many vertices does it have? Could a 3-regular graph have 5 vertices?}
prompt_plain: A simple graph is 3-regular (every vertex has degree 3) and has 12 edges. How many vertices does it have? Could a 3-regular graph have 5 vertices?

prompt_parts.text: A simple graph is 3-regular (every vertex has degree 3) and has 12 edges. How many vertices does it have? Could a 3-regular graph have 5 vertices?

worked_solution: Handshake lemma: the sum of all degrees equals 2 × (number of edges)
Sum of degrees = 2·12 = 24
Each vertex contributes 3, so 3v = 24 and v = 8
With v = 5 the degree sum would be 15, which is odd
The degree sum is always even, so no 3-regular graph has 5 vertices
final_answer: 8 vertices; no, 5 vertices would force an odd degree sum of 15

worked_solution: Let i be the number of internal vertices; the total number of vertices is n = i + 10
A tree on n vertices has n − 1 edges
Each internal vertex has exactly 2 children, so the number of edges is 2i
So i + 10 − 1 = 2i, which gives i = 9
Total vertices = 9 + 10 = 19 (and 18 edges)

prompt_latex: \text{Weighted graph on } A,B,C,D,E \text{ with edges } AB{=}4,\ AC{=}2,\ BC{=}1,\ BD{=}5,\ CD{=}8,\ CE{=}10,\ DE{=}2. \text{ Find a minimum spanning tree by Kruskal's algorithm and its weight.}
prompt_plain: Weighted graph on vertices A, B, C, D, E with edges AB = 4, AC = 2, BC = 1, BD = 5, CD = 8, CE = 10, DE = 2. Use Kruskal's algorithm to find a minimum spanning tree and its total weight.

prompt_parts.text: Weighted graph on vertices A, B, C, D, E with edges AB = 4, AC = 2, BC = 1, BD = 5, CD = 8, CE = 10, DE = 2. Use Kruskal's algorithm to find a minimum spanning tree and its total weight.

worked_solution: Sort the edges by weight: BC 1, AC 2, DE 2, AB 4, BD 5, CD 8, CE 10
Take BC (1): joins B and C
Take AC (2): joins A to {B, C}
Take DE (2): joins D and E, a separate component
Skip AB (4): A and B are already connected, it would form a cycle
Take BD (5): joins {A, B, C} to {D, E}. Now 4 edges connect all 5 vertices, so stop
final_answer: MST edges BC, AC, DE, BD with total weight 10
